Current ideation present; intent absent; plan absent; access reviewed true. Disposition: Outpatient care with close follow-up. He has passive thoughts that it would be easier not to wake up, without intent, plan or preparation; the self-injury during the episode happened in confusion and without suicidal intent. His risk is higher in the months after a first episode of psychosis, while he is depressed, and while he is drinking. A written safety plan was made with him, with his own early warning signs (nights with little sleep, hearing voices, drinking more, pulling away from his friend) and what to do about each. Lethal-means counseling: he has no firearm and no access to one and agreed not to acquire one; medicines are dispensed two weeks at a time; he will keep alcohol out of the house while he is low. The 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline was given and saved in his phone, with the clinic number. Safety reviewed at every visit.

text.div:
SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD

  • Continue the antipsychotic started in hospital at the lowest effective dose, with side-effect checks at each visit (akathisia, stiffness, sedation) and monitoring to the APA and ADA/APA standard: weight at every visit, blood pressure, fasting glucose, A1c and lipids at baseline, 12 weeks and yearly, and the AIMS at baseline and every six months
  • Psychiatry consultation with the first-episode psychosis coordinated specialty care team to review the provisional diagnosis and differential, the dose, the alcohol plan, and the workup for epilepsy
  • First-episode workup: blood count, metabolic panel, liver tests, thyroid test, vitamin B12, HIV and syphilis tests, urine drug test, brain MRI, and a sleep-deprived EEG because of the confusion and the question of seizures
  • Alcohol care: AUDIT-C, PEth at each check to follow drinking, brief counseling with goals he chooses, thiamine, and a medicine for alcohol use disorder once the liver tests are reviewed
  • Coordinated specialty care: a care coordinator, individual resilience-focused therapy, education about psychosis for him and for the people he chooses, support to return to painting and selling his work, and a peer specialist
  • Sleep as treatment and as an early warning sign: regular sleep and wake times, no alcohol to get to sleep, less coffee after noon, and a plan to call the team after two nights of short sleep
  • Structured safety assessment, a written safety plan with early warning signs, lethal-means counseling, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, PHQ-9 at each visit, and safety review at every visit
  • Akathisia: aripiprazole back to 10 mg daily, propranolol 10 mg twice daily for a few weeks, and a check of restlessness and of safety at each visit until it settles

resource.title: Vincent van Gogh synthetic care plan
resource.description: Dignified, recovery-oriented primary care for a 35-year-old painter twelve days after discharge from a first psychiatric admission for psychosis with mood features: keeping the diagnosis provisional and stating the differential (bipolar I disorder with psychotic features, brief psychotic or schizophreniform disorder, alcohol withdrawal or alcohol-induced psychosis, and focal epilepsy), a first-episode workup with brain MRI and EEG, antipsychotic monitoring to the APA and ADA/APA standard (weight at every visit, blood pressure, fasting glucose, A1c and lipids at baseline and 12 weeks, akathisia and movement checks with the AIMS), recognizing and treating akathisia, AUDIT-C, PEth and naltrexone for alcohol use disorder, sleep as treatment and as an early warning sign, coordinated specialty care, and a structured safety assessment with lethal-means counseling and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline reviewed at every visit, on the APA 1883 schizophrenia guideline, the CANMAT and ISBD bipolar guidelines, and the CMID depression and bipolar monograph.
